features.title: Page and controller routing
features.summary: Each directory under `client/pages` is one page path. On the server, controllers (classes that answer requests) go in `server/controllers`. Their route annotations give the paths.

features.title: Path variables
features.summary: A route path can hold a path variable, such as `{id}` in `GetRoute("/{id}")`. A path variable is a part of the URL that can change, such as an ID. `FromPath` puts its value into the method parameter with the same name. The parameter type is checked first. When `id` is a number, `/items/abc` gets 400. On the Tac side, a page folder whose name starts with an underscore, such as `client/pages/items/_id/`, matches any value. The view passes `page.path` to a service method, which reads the last segment. So every service language can use the value: a service in a language other than JavaScript or TypeScript has no DOM, but its methods take arguments from the view. A Python service also needs the `tac.python` runtime setting in `client/manifest.json`.

features.title: Shared data and the page
features.summary: A view (the HTML template of a page or component) reads `client/shared/data/<name>.json` as `data.<name>`. It reads the path of its document as `page.path`. It reads whether it runs in development mode as `page.development`. No service (a class that holds the state and behavior of a view) is needed (ADR 0036). Put content that has no behavior in these data files, not in a service. If the file is missing, the build fails with `TY1311`. No service may use `data` or `page` as its instance name.

A Python service also needs the `tac.python` runtime setting in `client/manifest.json`.

A Python service also needs the `tac.python` runtime setting in `client/manifest.json`.

features.title: Service classes
features.summary: A service is a class that holds the state and behavior of a view. A view refers to a service by its instance name: `BasketService` is `basket`. `{basket.count}` reads a field, and `on:click="basket.add()"` calls a method. Fields hold the state of the view. Methods give its behavior. By default, a service is a page singleton (one shared instance for the whole page). Every component that names it shares that one instance. `NeedsAll` creates one service instance for each component instance. It uses the properties of that component. `Lifetime({"value":"prototype"})` also gives other services one instance for each component. `OnStart` runs after injection (the framework gives the service the objects it needs). It also waits until the component is attached to the DOM (the tree of elements on the page). `OnStop` cleans up work that the service owns. A declared `applicationEventPublisher` field and `OnEvent` replace local publish and subscribe code that you would write by hand. A `Needs` field named after a browser resource receives that resource. There is no general framework object on the instance. Ordinary imports and helper functions still work. Constants are static class fields. A Python service writes `@on_start`, `@on_stop` and `@on_event` above synchronous methods, and its `application_event_publisher: ApplicationEventPublisher` field is the publisher. A C++ service writes `[[OnStart]]` and `[[OnEvent]]`, and its `ApplicationEventPublisher applicationEventPublisher;` field is the publisher.

features.title: Shared behavior annotations
features.summary: Tac and Yon share these annotations across their supported languages. The role, injection and description annotations are `Service`, `Helper`, `HTTPClient`, `Store`, `Converter`, `Setup`, `Lifetime`, `Needs`, `Named` and `Description`. Injection means the framework gives a class the objects it needs. The caching, data and resilience annotations are `CacheSettings`, `Cached`, `UpdateCache`, `ClearCache`, `PageDefaults`, `Retry`, `MaxAtOnce`, `AllOrNothing`, `Entity`, `Id`, `Table` and `Query`. `HTTP request annotations`, `Convert` and `Schedule` cover outgoing HTTP calls, mapping values and scheduling. The configuration annotations are `Settings`, `WhenProfile`, `WhenSetting` and `Setting`. The validation annotations are `Checked`, `Check`, `Required`, `NotEmpty`, `Length`, `Min` and `Max`. The test annotations are `Test`, `TestSetup`, `UseProfiles`, `TestSettings`, `Fake`, `FreshStart` and `ValueSource`, and a test case checks its result with `Assert`. Write each marker (annotation) on its own line. Marker options use strict JSON. The compiler turns the markers into runtime code inside the same source file. It does not use a reflection scanner (code that inspects classes while the program runs). The markers are global, so no language needs to import them, and the old `tachyon:behaviors` import fails the build with `TY1308` (ADR 0046). Native services use typed adapters with no embedded JavaScript. Tac stays client-only, and Yon stays REST-only. Each adapter has one clear owner. Queries have limits and must be authorized. The cache changes only after a call succeeds. Data transfer object (DTO) validation is pure: it has no side effects. Configuration keys start with the prefix of their realm: `TAC_` or `tac.` for Tac, and `YON_` or `yon.` for Yon. You give this configuration yourself. Markers with no arguments can be written without parentheses, as in Spring: `@Service`, `@Setup`, `@Needs`, `@Converter`. A plain `@Service` can be a Tac role or a Yon role. The folder that holds the file decides which one (ADR 0038). The service below needs no network or storage adapter. Role types must be in plural folders, and their file names must match their type names exactly. Collaborators are classes that a service works with. Tac finds annotated collaborators in the same language under `client/services`, `client/stores`, `client/remotes`, `client/setups`, `client/entities`, `client/helpers` and `client/converters`. Yon uses matching folders under `server/`. Controllers go in `server/controllers`, and their route annotations give the path (ADR 0048). `Test` units go in `server/tests/<Name>Test.<ext>` or `client/tests/<Name>Test.<ext>`, and `ty test` runs them. On managed Yon roles, `Needs` finds the provider for each marked field. So you do not need to write a constructor by hand. `Named` chooses a provider when the field name does not identify it. A Tac store, client or converter that a service gets with `Needs` opens the context of its Setup itself. A service that puts a behavior annotation on its own method, like `page` below, creates its context in `OnStart` with `Behaviors.create`. Python, Lua and C++ have no tab here: the build refuses `PageDefaults` and the other behavior annotations in Python, Lua and C++ Tac code with `TY1308` (ADR 0093, ADR 0085, ADR 0099).

files.name: adapter ownership
files.code:
Configuration returns only application-selected caches/http/entities adapters.
Each behavior context belongs to one owner. Derive its partition
from authenticated ownership, or declare a fixed partition for public data.
Cache authorization must return literal true for hits, misses and eviction;
@CacheKey parameters must cover every input that changes a result. The adapter enforces
entry quotas and atomic replacement. Yon contexts do not survive requests.

Explicit repository CRUD adapters own authorization and tenancy.
Structured queries additionally require authorizeEntity(command, execution).
Entity adapters own parameterized operations.
HTTP adapters honor redirect: 'error', credentials: 'omit', cancellation,
deadlines and the bounded response while reading. Never bundle server
credentials in Tac. No annotation adds SSR or native capabilities.

Stores, clients and converters: a service asks for them with Needs.
A store or client opens the context of its Setup itself; a converter
needs no context. A service that uses a behavior annotation on its own
method creates its context in OnStart with Behaviors.create.
Yon managed roles: Needs finds each marked field's provider; no
handwritten constructor is necessary, and Named names the provider.
HTTPClient request methods (GetRequest, PostRequest, ...) return
JSON types or models; annotations cannot rewrite a method or
constructor signature.

files.name: bounded query and cache policies
files.code:
Store(Entity, {fields, defaultSize, maxSize}) is a contract with no
implementation, like a Spring Data repository interface. A Store without
an Entity is refused (TY1308). Referenced Entity/Table and query classes
use exact role filenames in their realm's shared role folder. Methods
without a body become find/count/exists commands; derived
findByStatus/countByStatus/existsByStatus are supported.
Predicates combine with AND; no SQL, OR, joins or arbitrary expressions.
authorizeEntity(command, execution) must return true before adapter execute.
Find is bounded to page size <=100 with annotation-owned ordering and
an ID tie-breaker. Caller page.sort must be empty. Results stay bounded JSON.

UpdateCache/ClearCache({method: 'find'}) target a same-class Cached method
and match its key parameters by name. Its page input and key policy are reused. Authorization
and key/adapter checks precede mutation; store/delete follows successful
bounded output and lifetime checks. Put never reads. No atomic database/cache
transaction, automatic reconciliation, retry or AllOrNothing is promised.
Annotation object options must be written as strict JSON.

files.name: configuration and validation boundaries
files.code:
Settings binds explicit nested tac/yon snapshots into typed JSON.
Each underscore in prefixed names maps to a path segment; no ambient environment access.
Unknown selected-prefix keys fail. Setting binds one field by path from the parsed application configuration
through Behaviors.values; Tac may name only tac.*, Yon only yon.*.
WhenProfile/WhenSetting inspect
snapshotted explicit inputs before configure. Never ship server secrets to Tac.

Checked marks direct DTO fields. Required/NotEmpty require values;
Length counts UTF-8 string bytes or array/object entries. Min/Max accept finite
numbers without coercion. Length/Min/Max otherwise ignore missing/null.
Check validates the selected method argument before pagination/cache/HTTP/body.
Behaviors.validate(Type, value) needs no context or DTO construction.
Errors expose redacted field/rule paths. Unknown fields remain allowed.
No nested groups or automatic field assignment; validate again in Yon.

features.title: Styles next to each view
features.summary: A `tac.css` file next to a component view is the stylesheet of that component. A component folder holds only its view and its stylesheet. A page holds no CSS file in any folder (`TY1309`). The compiler wraps the stylesheet in CSS `@scope`, which limits styles to one part of the page. The scope starts at the component and stops at every nested component, also one without a stylesheet and one placed in a slot. So the rules of a parent never style a child component. Tachyon does not rewrite selectors. Component HTML cannot hold a `<style>` element or a stylesheet link (`TY1403`). Global colors, fonts, custom properties and resets go in the stylesheets that `tac.styles` lists in `client/manifest.json`; layout and animation stay in the component's `tac.css`. A third-party stylesheet is declared in `tac.styleSources` with its package, exact version, license and SHA-256. Other global CSS stops the build with `TY1403`. A Python service also needs the `tac.python` runtime setting in `client/manifest.json`.

features.title: Caching public reads
features.summary: A service reads the network only through an `HTTPClient`; a JavaScript or TypeScript service that calls `fetch` itself fails to build with `TY1361`. To keep a read, put the cache annotations that services use on the client, as Spring's `@Cacheable` works on any bean: `CacheSettings` on the client class names the cache and its limits, `Cached` on a read keeps its answer (with `CacheKey` on the arguments that pick the answer), and `ClearCache` or `UpdateCache` on a write removes or replaces that answer after the write succeeds. This works the same in every language that has an `HTTPClient`. Python and Lua have no tab here, because the build refuses `HTTPClient` in Python and Lua Tac code with `TY1308`. In JavaScript and TypeScript, Tachyon's browser transport also sends a `Cached` GET as a public read, so the service worker may answer it. A service worker is a browser script that can answer requests from a cache. The manifest's `tac.cache` sets the worker's policy for each path: `cache-first`, `network-first` or `no-store`. A path without a rule is not kept by the worker. The worker keeps a read only when it has no `Authorization` header and the response is cacheable; a response with `private`, `no-store` or `Vary` is not kept, and a successful write removes the entries under its path. After `ClearCache` or `UpdateCache`, the next uncached JavaScript or TypeScript GET revalidates the browser HTTP cache, even when the server sent a long public `max-age`; a cache-first worker rule also asks the network for that read. A read that is not `Cached` is sent `no-store`, so it is always fresh. A GET that sends an `Authorization` header is never kept in the browser HTTP cache, even when it is `Cached`. Dart, Rust, Go, Kotlin, Swift, Java, Ruby, C# and F# clients use the same browser transport when their Setup has no HTTP adapter for the client. C++ has an `HTTPClient` but no tab here, because the build refuses `Cached` in C++ Tac code with `TY1308` (ADR 0099). In the compiled examples below, the Setup's HTTP adapter answers inside the page, so the worker never sees the request, and `Cached` keeps the answer in the page. The old `cache` option of `@HTTPClient` is replaced by `Cached` (ADR 0087).

The WebAssembly service uses the same companion protocol (ADR 0035, ADR 0037, ADR 0045). Views read its fields, methods receive JSON arguments, and `Service` and `NeedsAll` are declared above its type. JavaScript and TypeScript services are not WebAssembly: the browser runs them as JavaScript, so this page has no JavaScript or TypeScript tab (see "Polyglot native services" for them).

features.title: REST controllers
features.summary: A controller is a class in `server/controllers/` that answers HTTP requests. `RequestRoute` on the class gives its path, and `Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)` says who may call it. `GetRoute`, `PostRoute` and the other route annotations mark the methods that answer. Each method name starts with its verb, such as `getProducts`. A returned model, or a list of models, becomes JSON with the model's field names. `ResponseStatus(201)` sets the status code. `FromBody` reads the JSON body into a model (a data type in `server/models/`). A body that does not fit the model gets 400 before the method runs. To set the status, headers and body yourself, answer with the language's own response: a Fetch `Response` in JavaScript and TypeScript, an `(HTTPStatus, headers, body)` tuple in Python, a `[status, headers, body]` array in Ruby, a `{ status, headers, body }` table in Lua, `http_response_code()`, `header()` and `echo` in PHP, the same `HttpExchange` in Java, Groovy and Kotlin, `HttpResponseMessage` in C# and F#, `http::Response` in Rust, a shelf `Response` in Dart and `*http.Response` in Go. If you return `text/html` yourself, Yon passes it through unchanged. Yon never renders it. A controller needs no framework import, base class, registration call or package.

features.title: Relaying to Perl and other programs
features.summary: Yon supports controllers in many languages. A route method can return `relay(command, request)` to call another program that implements Handler Protocol v1. `request` is the method parameter without a marker. It is the request in the language's own type, and `relay` answers with the language's own response. In PHP, `Yon::relay(command)` forwards the current request. The application gives the command at the call site. Tachyon supervises the program. It limits the program to the time left in the request and to the process limits. It gives the program only the baseline environment and the names on the allowlist (a list of allowed names). No shell execution is needed. To call one method and get a value back, use `@Gateway`. Lua has no tab here, because the build refuses `relay` in Lua Yon code with `TY2015` (ADR 0085): write the controller that relays in another Yon language.

The helper is supplied by Yon and needs no package or import.

  Java        Yon.relay(java.util.List.of("perl", "server/relays/report.pl"), exchange);
  Groovy      Yon.relay(java.util.List.of("perl", "server/relays/report.pl"), exchange)
  Kotlin      Yon.relay(listOf("perl", "server/relays/report.pl"), exchange)

inherits the request deadline, validates protocol frames, and reaps

features.title: Middleware
features.summary: Middleware is code that runs around every request. One middleware file at the project root runs before every request and again after the response. It can reject a request, or change or replace the response of the controller. Who may call a route is decided by the route itself (`Public`, `SignedIn`, `Allow(Role)`) and the one identity provider, not by middleware.

    }

open System.Net.Http

type Middleware =
    static member before(request: HttpRequestMessage) : HttpResponseMessage =
        let token = request.Headers.Authorization
        let signedIn = not (isNull token) && token.ToString() = "let-me-in"
        if request.RequestUri.AbsolutePath.StartsWith("/private") && not signedIn then
            let body = new StringContent("{\"error\":\"Unauthorized\"}", Encoding.UTF8, "application/json")
            new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.Unauthorized, Content = body)
        else
            null

    static member after(request: HttpRequestMessage) : HttpResponseMessage =
        let response = new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.NoContent)
        response.Headers.Add("x-served-by", "tachyon")
        response

features.title: Generated route schemas
features.summary: Tachyon makes a schema (a description of the data shape) for every route from the controller code. It reads the path variables, the query values, the headers, the body and the return type from the method signature. A model (a data type in `server/models/`) describes a body or an answer. JavaScript writes its types in JSDoc comments (this example imports the TypeScript model), Ruby types its method with YARD tags, and Lua with LuaLS `---@param` and `---@return` comments. Tachyon checks every marked parameter before the method runs. A value that does not fit gets 400, and so does a body with a field that the model does not declare: every model schema says `"additionalProperties": false`. An answer that does not match the return type gets 500. The server answers `OPTIONS` with the `Allow` header and the route schema. `/api.json` lists every route and model in one document, with the version of Tachyon that built it, and `/api-docs/` shows the same document as a page. The outputs here come from the TypeScript tab. Each language writes its own types, so an integer type such as Lua's `integer` becomes `"type": "integer"`, and `/items/abc` then gets "must be a whole number". You write no schema file. The schema is public: `OPTIONS` and `/api.json` describe a route even when the route itself needs a signed-in user.

features.title: Streaming controllers
features.summary: StreamRoute marks a controller method that answers GET requests with a stream of server-sent events (SSE). The method produces many values, one at a time, with the language's own `yield` syntax, and its name starts with `stream`. It keeps the loop in a private generator method and only passes on that method's values. Tachyon sends each value as one limited event, and an end event when the method finishes. In the browser, StreamRequest on an HTTPClient method receives the stream. Tachyon opens it when a component first uses the client, opens it again after 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds when it fails (at most five tries in a row), and closes it with the component. Sixty seconds with no message also counts as a failure, so a silent stream is opened again. Each message is checked against the model type of the method's one parameter, passed to the method, and published as that model's event, so an OnEvent listener in any Tac language receives it. The StreamRequest client is JavaScript, TypeScript, Go or Kotlin. A Go client is an interface method such as `Receive(tick Tick)`; the page holds the stream for the Go service that keeps the client in a `// @Needs` field, and the service receives each message with `// @OnEvent`. A Kotlin client is an interface method such as `fun receive(tick: Tick)`, held the same way for the Kotlin web service that keeps it in a `@Needs` field. Dart, Rust, Ruby, Python, Lua, Swift, Java, C#, F# and C++ refuse StreamRequest with TY1308. A Lua stream method sends each value with `coroutine.yield`, and a Go stream method returns an `iter.Seq` whose function calls `yield`. On the server, Java, Groovy and Rust cannot stream, because they have no native generator, so they refuse StreamRoute with TY2015. Like every route, a stream says who may call it with `Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)`.

Which languages a stream is written in

  .js, .ts   an async generator
  .py        a generator
  .php       a generator, framed by the prelude
  .kt        a Sequence, framed by the prelude
  .cs        an IEnumerable or IAsyncEnumerable, framed
             by the prelude
  .fs        a seq or IAsyncEnumerable, framed by the prelude
  .dart      an async* Stream, framed by the prelude
  .rb        a method that yields, framed by the runner
  .lua       a method that calls coroutine.yield, framed by
             the runner
  .go        an iter.Seq or iter.Seq2 iterator, framed by
             the prelude

Every Yon language with a generator streams. A stream is a route method that answers more
than once, and native generator syntax produces it.
Each language adapter or protocol prelude keeps that generator open
and emits one bounded frame per value.

Java, Groovy and Rust are deliberately single-response because
none of them has a native generator. Tachyon refuses StreamRoute on
them (TY2015). A streaming route can use any generator-capable Yon
language.

In one controller, either every GET route is a StreamRoute or none is.

A Go stream that can fail returns iter.Seq2[Model, error]; the
first error ends the stream, and the browser gets event: error
without the error text. A stream has the request
time limit: at the limit the server stops it and sends
event: error, and the browser opens the stream again.

In the browser, @StreamRequest is JavaScript, TypeScript, Go or
Kotlin. A Go client is an interface method such as
Receive(tick Tick), and a Kotlin client is one such as
fun receive(tick: Tick); the page holds the stream for the Go or
Kotlin web service that keeps the client in a @Needs field, and
that service receives each message with @OnEvent.

JavaScript and TypeScript require a runtime supporting the authored
stream syntax; Node is the default. Other languages still require
their supported interpreter or compiler toolchain.

features.title: Socket controllers
features.summary: SocketRoute marks a controller class that keeps a WebSocket open, as Jakarta's @ServerEndpoint does. Tachyon makes one object of the class for each connection, so its fields hold that connection's state. OnOpen, OnMessage, OnClose and OnError mark the methods that run when a browser connects, sends a message, leaves, or when a method fails. Each message is JSON text, and Tachyon checks it against the model type of the OnMessage parameter first. The session sends messages back, and openSessions() (open_sessions() in Python, Ruby, Lua and Rust, OpenSessions() in Go, C# and F#, getOpenSessions() in Java) returns every open connection of the same path, so one message can go to every tab. In Go, session.Request() returns the request that opened the socket as an *http.Request, with the query string and the headers. When OnOpen or OnMessage fails, OnError runs and the socket stays open, as in Jakarta. In the browser, SocketRequest on an HTTPClient method receives the messages and publishes each one as its model's event, and the client's send(message) writes to the socket. The SocketRequest client is JavaScript, TypeScript, Go or Kotlin. A Go client is an interface method such as `Receive(message ChatMessage)`; the page holds the socket for the Go service that keeps the client in a `// @Needs` field, the service receives each message with `// @OnEvent`, and the generated `Send(message any) error` writes to the socket and returns an error code such as `HTTP_NETWORK` instead of a rejected promise. A Kotlin client is an interface method such as `fun receive(message: ChatMessage)`; the page holds the socket for the Kotlin web service that keeps the client in a `@Needs` field, and the generated `suspend fun send(message: Any)` waits for the page and throws an error whose message starts with the code, such as `HTTP_NETWORK`. Dart, Rust, Ruby, Python, Lua, Swift, Java, C#, F# and C++ refuse SocketRequest with TY1308, and their services receive the messages with OnEvent. Sockets are written in any Yon language. Tachyon guards every socket (ADR 0060): a message is JSON text of at most 64 KiB; a message that is not JSON or does not fit the model closes the socket with code 1007, a binary message with 1003, and a larger message with 1009. Five minutes without a message closes it with 1001, a socket lasts at most one hour, and a page from another origin gets 403. `Public`, `SignedIn` or `Allow(Role)` on the class says who may connect; Tachyon answers 401 or 403 before it opens the socket.

Every Yon language holds a socket. Tachyon keeps one handler
process running for the whole connection, and the runner or
prelude of each language reads the socket's message frames while
the class runs. Each language names the session methods in its
own style (above). In Go, session.Request() returns the request
that opened the socket as an *http.Request, with the query string
and the headers. A method that throws, panics or returns an
error counts as a failure. In Rust the object is shared, so its
fields keep state in a Cell or a lock.

When OnOpen or OnMessage fails, OnError runs and the socket stays
open, as in Jakarta. The error text goes to the server log only.

In the browser, @SocketRequest is JavaScript, TypeScript, Go or
Kotlin. Every Tac language receives the messages with @OnEvent. A
Go client is an interface method; the page holds the socket for the
Go service that keeps the client in a // @Needs field, and the
generated Send(message any) error returns HTTP_NETWORK when 16
messages already wait for the socket to open. A Kotlin client is an
interface method such as fun receive(message: ChatMessage); the
page holds the socket for the Kotlin web service that keeps the
client in a @Needs field, and the generated suspend send(message)
throws an error whose message starts with HTTP_NETWORK in that case.

Limits: messages are JSON text of at most 64 KiB, at most 32
sockets are open at once, five idle minutes or one hour close a
socket, and only pages from the same origin may open it. A
socket path has no {variables}; send the value in a message.

What the browser gets when a rule is broken:

  403   the page comes from another origin
  426   a plain HTTP request asks for the socket path
  503   32 sockets are already open; try again later
  1007  the message is not JSON, or does not fit the model
  1003  the message is binary data, not JSON text
  1009  the message is larger than 64 KiB
  1001  the socket was idle for five minutes, the browser went
        away, or the server is stopping

The route list in /api.json and the OPTIONS answer of the path
mark a socket with "socket": true. When a socket closes with
another code, the browser client opens it again after 1, 2, 4, 8
and 16 seconds. It does not open it again after 1000, 1003, 1007
or 1009. While the socket is not open, send(message) keeps at
most 16 messages and sends them when the socket opens.

features.title: Inject an OS file picker into a service
features.summary: A service asks for the operating system's file picker by injection. `tac.nativeCapabilities: ["filePicker"]` in `client/manifest.json` grants it, separately from `tac.browserApis`. Without the grant, every call answers `denied` before a panel opens. The grant does not replace the user's choice or the signing entitlements: a sandboxed macOS app also needs the user-selected read-only file entitlement, and Tachyon does not add it for you. `open` lets the user choose one file; the only type filters are `text/plain` and `application/json`, and an empty list allows any file. The answer holds the file name and an opaque handle, never a path. `readText(handle)` reads at most 65,536 bytes of UTF-8 text, and `release(handle)` ends access. A handle belongs to the service that asked for it. It ends after 300 seconds, or sooner when that service goes away. Every answer is a typed status (`selected`, `cancelled`, `read`, `released`, `denied`, `unsupported`, `unavailable`, `invalid`, `disposed` or `tooLarge`); nothing throws. The picker opens a panel (NSOpenPanel) only in a macOS app, for JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust and Swift services (ADR 0089). A browser tab and the iOS, Android, Linux and Windows apps open no panel and answer `unsupported`. JavaScript and TypeScript inject `filePicker` with `@Needs` and get Promises. Rust declares a `FilePicker` field in a `Default` service. Swift, C# and Kotlin ask for an uninitialized `FilePicker` field with `NeedsAll`. Every service uses the same file on every target. Where a Swift, C# or Kotlin service runs as WebAssembly in the page (the web, and targets that do not link the language: Swift on Linux, Windows and Android, C# off Windows, Kotlin off Android), the field is still filled: `available()` is false and every call answers `unsupported`. Options that break the contract, such as more than one file or another type, still answer `invalid`. The page never passes a `filePicker` property. Dart, Go, Ruby, Java, F# and Python services have no FilePicker provider yet, so this feature has no tab for them; a `NeedsAll` FilePicker field there stays a page property, and the build stops with `TY1407` when the page does not pass it. A Lua service has no FilePicker: a `---@type FilePicker` field in a Lua service stops the build with `TY2015`. A C++ `Needs` field may name only a C++ service or a C++ `HTTPClient`, so C++ has no FilePicker either (`TY1372`). Let a JavaScript, TypeScript or Rust service use the picker and send the text to the other services with an event.

features.title: Compiled services publish to the page
features.summary: Native services, WebAssembly services and TypeScript or Dart browser services inject an `ApplicationEventPublisher` for local events. `OnEvent` receives the events, and `OnStart`/`OnStop` run when the service starts and stops. Call the publisher to publish an event. A listener that is not `InBackground` can also return a model value. The runtime then publishes it as the model named by the return type of the listener. Each activation gets a new ID. The runtime rejects callbacks from an old activation. Each example publishes a `CatalogCount` model when it starts and updates its count in a listener for that model. Ruby names the model of a listener in a YARD tag, # @param value [CatalogCount]. Lua names it in a LuaCATS tag, ---@param value CatalogCount, and publishes a model table, setmetatable({ count = 5 }, CatalogCount), through its application_event_publisher field. F# takes the publisher as a constructor parameter, `type CatalogService(applicationEventPublisher: ApplicationEventPublisher)`. Python declares an `application_event_publisher: ApplicationEventPublisher` field, names the model of a listener in its type hint, `value: CatalogCount`, and publishes a dataclass, `CatalogCount(5)`. C++ declares an `ApplicationEventPublisher applicationEventPublisher;` field, takes the model as `const CatalogCount& value` in its `[[OnEvent]]` method, and publishes `CatalogCount{5}`. The JavaScript `CatalogService` only listens, to events published by its native or WebAssembly counterpart.

features.title: The ty binary
features.summary: One standalone executable creates projects (`ty init` asks what the app should have and installs the missing tools; `ty add` grows the app later), runs them in development, builds them and inspects them. `ty preview` is the development server for Tac and Yon. `ty bundle` is the release build: it writes the files that you publish, and `ty start` serves them without building them again. `ty handler invoke` runs one controller or worker through the protocol, without any server. It binds controller arguments like the server does, but it skips the route access rules, so keep it a local operator tool. `ty test` compiles and runs the `Test` units of the project in both realms (Tac and Yon). It also reports the public methods of annotated classes that no test case called. `ty migrate fix` updates a project after a breaking change in Tachyon. It only prints the changes and the manual steps; `--write` writes them. For example, it rewrites `<if :when>`, `<else>` and `<for :each>` in views to `<logic>` and `<loop>` (`TY1367`), and it moves `client/utils/` to `client/shared/utils/` and changes the import paths. It moves files only inside `client/` and `server/`, never overwrites a file and never follows a symbolic link. It deletes only an old route file that has no code left and the old `tachyon.json` after it moves its settings into `client/manifest.json`. `ty migrate check` lists what ty does not support. A file that is not UTF-8 text is one finding, and the check goes on with the other files.

Its `tac` member holds the application identity and window, page metadata, shared browser assets, service-worker cache rules and the sitemap settings. It is data, so every build reads it the same way without running code. features.title: Toolchain checks
features.summary: `ty doctor` checks whether this machine can build and run the project. It reports only the toolchains (compilers and build tools) and controller runtimes that the project uses. `--json` prints the same report in a format for other programs. Each row is `ready`, `partial` (found, but too old or not complete), `missing`, or `info`. `info` is a tool that the project can do without: a native companion compiler (Swift, Kotlin, Rust or C# for a native target), TinyGo, or `wasm-opt`. `ty doctor` exits with 0 when every needed toolchain is ready, and with 1 when a needed toolchain is missing or too old, or the project cannot be read. `info` rows do not change the exit status. A service that runs as WebAssembly needs these checks. TypeScript: `tsc` 6 or newer, from the project's `node_modules/.bin` or from PATH. Rust: the `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target. Go: Go 1.27 or newer; TinyGo 0.42 or newer makes release modules several times smaller, and without it the build uses the standard Go compiler. C# and F#: the .NET `wasm-tools` workload (the row is named "C# services on the web"). Kotlin: `kotlinc-js` 2.1.10 and the kotlin-stdlib-wasm-js 2.1.10 `.klib` file from Maven Central; set `TAC_KOTLIN_WASM_STDLIB` to that file. Swift: Swift 6.3.3 from swift.org (not Xcode's `swiftc`) and the matching Swift SDK for WebAssembly from `swift sdk install`; set `TAC_SWIFT_WASM_SDK` to its `wasm32-unknown-wasip1` folder, and set `TAC_SWIFT_WASM_COMPILER` to the swift.org `swiftc` when another `swiftc` comes first on PATH. Kotlin and Swift show `partial` without `wasm-opt`, because their release modules would be much larger. Java: `javac` from a JDK 21 or newer and TeaVM 0.15.0. Dart: the Dart SDK 3.13 or newer. Ruby: Tachyon's Ruby WebAssembly runtime, which Tachyon builds once with Ruby, Emscripten 6.0.10 or newer (`emcc`) and a C compiler (`clang` on macOS, `gcc` elsewhere, or `CC`). Lua: Tachyon's Lua WebAssembly runtime, built once with Emscripten 6.0.10 or newer, and the `lua` program (5.4 or newer) for test units. When a runtime is already in the Tachyon cache, its row shows it as ready instead of the build tools. Python: the pinned Pyodide 314.0.7 runtime (CPython 3.14.2). Copy the five core files from the official `pyodide-core-314.0.7.tar.bz2` archive into the `python-web/314.0.7` folder of the Tachyon cache; ty checks the size and SHA-256 hash of each file and never downloads Python or Python packages. The project also needs `tac.python` in `client/manifest.json` with `"runtime": "pyodide-314.0.7"` and `"profile": "offline"`; without it the row shows `TY1605`. `wasm-opt` from Binaryen version_133 or newer makes the release WebAssembly of Rust, Go, Swift and Java smaller. For Yon, the report checks each runtime that the controllers use: `node`, or `bun` when `node` is not on `PATH` (`YON_JAVASCRIPT_RUNTIME`), `python3`, or `python` on Windows (`YON_PYTHON_RUNTIME`), `ruby` 3.3 or newer (`YON_RUBY_RUNTIME`), `java`, `groovyc` (Groovy 4 or newer, or `GROOVY_HOME`), `kotlinc`, `dotnet` for C# and F#, `rustc` and `cargo`, `dart`, `go` 1.27 or newer, `php-cgi` and `lua`. `ty doctor --install` offers to install each missing tool that Tachyon can install, the way `ty init` does (`--yes` installs them without asking). For TeaVM it downloads the five jars from Maven Central, checks each one against the SHA-256 that Tachyon pins, and keeps them in the Tachyon cache, never in the project. `TAC_TEAVM_HOME` still points at a folder of your own. Each check has its own time limit: 10 seconds, and 60 seconds for the C# check, because it builds a small project. So a busy machine does not report a working toolchain as broken. The development server and `ty test` run the same checks before they start. `ty --help` does not list `doctor`, but `ty doctor --help` prints its options and exit status.

features.title: What a page may do to its window
features.summary: `client/manifest.json` declares the native window. It also grants (allows) the window controls that a service may use, under `tac.application.window.controls`. By default, no control is granted. A service gets the controls by injection, like the other browser APIs: `@Needs windowControls` in JavaScript and TypeScript, and a `WindowControls` field in Rust, Go, C#, F#, Kotlin, Java, Dart, Ruby and Swift. The calls are `granted(control)`, `minimize()`, `maximize()`, `fullscreen()`, `close()`, `resize(width, height)` and `setTitle(text)`, written in each language's case (`set_title` in Rust and Ruby, `SetTitle` in Go, C# and F#). A call to a control that is not granted fails at once, and the message names the grant to add. In a browser tab, `granted` answers `false` and every call fails, because the page has no native window. The host (the native app that shows the page) checks each grant again before it acts. The macOS host runs the controls on the app's own window, and a macOS test checks this on a real app window. The Linux (GTK) host has the controls too, but no test calls them on a Linux desktop yet. On Windows, a test that needs the MSVC compiler builds the host's control code into a small program and drives a real Win32 window: it sets a granted title (with UTF-16 surrogate pairs), resizes the window, enters and leaves fullscreen and minimizes it, and checks that a close without its grant and a call from another thread are refused. That test does not open the full app or WebView2. The Android host registers its window adapter too, but it is only type-checked, not run on an Android device. The page has no `globalThis.tachyonWindow` global any more, and a service that reads `globalThis` fails to build with `TY1360`. A service that the native app links in has no page, but it gets the controls from the host with the same grants (ADR 0089). The Rust file shown here works in the page and when a macOS, Linux or Windows app links it, because Rust fills the field with `Default`. Swift on Apple platforms, C# on Windows and Kotlin on Android instead declare an uninitialized `WindowControls` field with `NeedsAll`. Their native files are under native/, a documentation folder; the file you choose goes in the application's client/services/. Native service code belongs to the application. It runs as normal operating-system code, and this window-control policy does not sandbox (limit) it. Lua, Python and C++ services have no `WindowControls` yet, so this feature has no tab for them: a Lua field of this type stops the build with `TY2015`, Python stops it with `TY1605` (`WindowControls` is not a model), and a C++ `Needs` field may name only a C++ service or a C++ `HTTPClient` (`TY1372`). Let a service in another language handle the window.

features.title: Request isolation
features.summary: By default, each request runs in one process with limits. With `YON_ISOLATION=firecracker`, Yon sends each supported request to a microVM control program. The deployment owns this program. A microVM is a small virtual machine. For now, this transport supports only JavaScript and Python controllers. A controller in another language fails before the driver starts. The handler protocol and the build do not change. Tachyon does not include the microVM program. It also does not yet claim that any microVM setup isolates requests safely.

files.name: isolation
files.code:
How a handler runs

  YON_ISOLATION=process       one supervised child process per
                              request. The default.

  YON_ISOLATION=firecracker   hand each request to a Firecracker
                              control program instead.

    YON_FIRECRACKER_DRIVER      the control program to run
    YON_FIRECRACKER_POOL        how many microVMs to keep
    YON_FIRECRACKER_VCPUS       vCPUs per microVM
    YON_FIRECRACKER_MEMORY_MIB  memory per microVM
    YON_FIRECRACKER_EGRESS      what a handler may reach

Read from the environment rather than a config file, because
which isolation a deployment wants is a property of where it
runs, not of the source — the same build runs either way.

An invalid or half-declared policy fails as TY2010 before a
handler runs, rather than falling back to something weaker than
what was asked for.

features.title: Serving what was published
features.summary: `ty start` serves a bundle that is already built. `server/application.json` and its profile files hold `yon` settings that are not secret. These files have no `yon` root key (top-level key). `.env` holds private Yon secrets. Public `tac` settings are already in the bundle. The deployment chooses the runtime executable and the isolation policy. `outgoing.hosts` in `server/application.json` lists the hosts that Yon code may call; at run time a local guard refuses every other host. `server.hosts` lists the names that a loopback server answers besides localhost names, IP addresses and the `tac.origin` host, such as the name that a reverse proxy sends.

Serving a built bundle

  client/manifest.json         web app manifest; its tac member is public Tac configuration
  server/application.json      non-secret yon namespace
  server/application-<profile>.json  Yon-only runtime profile overlay
  .env                         literal YON_ secrets; ignored by builds
  YON_PROFILE                  parent profile selector
  YON_APPLICATION_JSON         reserved private output to Yon children
  /manifest.webmanifest        the published manifest, tac member included
  TAC_DIST_PATH                existing bundle location
  YON_JAVASCRIPT_RUNTIME       JavaScript runtime (node)
  YON_PYTHON_RUNTIME           Python runtime (python3; python on Windows)
  YON_RUBY_RUNTIME             Ruby runtime (ruby, 3.3 or newer)
  TAC_CACHE_DIR                standalone runtime cache location

CLI host/port > profile > base file > command defaults.
No parent application-setting or secret overrides.
Underscores map paths: YON_CATALOG_PAGE_SIZE -> yon.catalog.page.size.
Restart Yon after changing private settings or .env.
Configured datasource/Redis resources are managed per Yon server.
Inject DataSource or RedisTemplate with Needs; schema changes stay explicit.

features.title: What a project looks like
features.summary: A project has two directories: `client` and `server`. Each page route is a folder under `client/pages` that holds a `tac.html` file. Server controllers live in `server/controllers`, and their annotations give the routes. Page behavior is in service classes under `client/services`. Application helpers are ordinary code in their language. Role types for `Allow`, such as `Admin`, are empty classes in `server/roles`, and the one `IdentityProvider` class lives in `server/controllers`.

files.name: layout
files.code:
What `ty init` lays out

  client/
    pages/          one folder per route, holding a tac.html
    components/     a two-level path, <product-card>: a view and its styles
    services/       one <Name>Service class per file, addressed as {name.field}
    tests/          <Name>Test files run by ty test
    shared/         published as-is: assets/, data/, styles/ and scripts/;
                    utility classes go in shared/utils/
    manifest.json   name, icons, start_url, and in tac: the
                    application identity and window, metadata,
                    shared assets, cache rules and the sitemap

  server/
    controllers/    <Name>Controller classes; their annotations give the routes
    tests/          <Name>Test files run by ty test
    data/           files a controller reads or writes
    deps/           starts empty
    application.json  Yon configuration without secrets

  Folders you add when you need them, in client/ and server/:
    models/         data types
    remotes/        HTTPClient contracts that send requests
    stores/  setups/  entities/  helpers/  converters/  services/

  Only in server/:
    roles/          empty role classes that @Allow names
    gateways/       reserved: Tachyon generates @Gateway units here, never
                    write files in it

tac.html, client/services and the role folders are framework contracts:
a role-annotated type is found by the folder it sits in and the file name
that matches its type (ADR 0031). models/ holds data types only
(ADR 0041, ADR 0043), and tests/ is where ty test looks. Tachyon no
longer reads server/routes/ (TY1310).
